_comment: lab.json - the main source of the lab's data: domain, networks, the lab VMs and what is
published to your PC. Read by vagrant/Vagrantfile (Ruby JSON.parse) to create the lab VMs, by
scripts/commands/firewall.ps1 (ConvertFrom-Json) to render the OPNsense configuration (DHCP
reservations, DNS names, virtual IPs, port forwards), by scripts/commands/up.ps1 (firewall
address, domain), by scripts/commands/down.ps1 (vms: which leftover Hyper-V folders it may
delete) and by scripts/commands/deploy.ps1 and lab.ps1 deploy matrix (domain: the URLs of
their checks and messages).
Copies kept by hand, to change together with this file: the PC address, DNS server and NRPT
namespace in scripts/host/Initialize-LabHost.ps1; the domain in lab_domain
(ansible/inventory/group_vars/all.yml) and in matrix_domain and the Matrix inventory's host
name (ansible/matrix/inventory/); the matrix entry's published address as
livekit_server_config_rtc_node_ip in ansible/matrix/inventory/host_vars/.../vars.yml.
vms: the Ubuntu VMs behind the firewall (built by Vagrant). New VMs are created by
lab.ps1 up. firewall-nginx.yml adds nginx and reconciles the managed ingress forwards
on an existing firewall; other new VMs still need a firewall rebuild for DHCP and DNS.
mac: 12 hex digits without separators, as Hyper-V expects; 02 marks a locally administered
address. By convention the last four bytes are the VM's IP in hex (0a0a0a1e = 10.10.10.30).
cpus/memory (MB): the VM's size in Hyper-V. A change is applied with "vagrant reload <vm>" in
the vagrant folder (the VM restarts).
checkpoints (default true): false disables Hyper-V checkpoints. A checkpoint of a running VM
saves its RAM to disk; for vault that RAM holds the unsealed OpenBao keys.
consoleAutologin (default true): false keeps the normal login prompt on the Hyper-V console
(no password-less root shell for whoever opens the console of vault).
network (default LabNet): the name of a segment (below) the VM lives in instead.
segments: further networks behind the firewall, each with its own private Hyper-V switch,
firewall interface (opt2/hn3, opt3/hn4, ... in this order), address, DHCP range and filter
rules. scripts/lib/LabNetwork.ps1 checks them, scripts/lib/LabFirewall.ps1 renders them into
the firewall; a new segment needs lab.ps1 firewall -Rebuild (the firewall gets an adapter).
k8s: the Kubernetes cluster (RKE2 with Cilium, Rancher Manager; ansible/kubernetes/). Its
nodes may use only DNS on the firewall and the internet; from LabNet only
ansible-control (SSH) and central nginx (the published web ports) reach into it.
published: what your PC may reach in the lab, per VM. Your PC never reaches a lab VM directly;
it reaches a published address on the firewall's HOST network, and the firewall forwards the
listed ports to the VM (destination NAT). A port's optional targetVm "nginx" sends it to
the central nginx ingress instead (only tcp 80 and 443). A publication with such a port is
routed: after route activation its names resolve to nginx inside the lab, and its VM keeps
its private address under <vm>-backend. Other publications (vault) stay direct. A port's
optional source "pc" limits it to the PC's address (default: any client on HOST).
opnsense/lab-nginx.php applies all of this to a running firewall (deploy nginx).
One address per service VM, because two VMs may need the same
port (443). Each name becomes <name>.lab.internal ("@" is lab.internal itself, as in DNS zone
files) with two addresses: your PC gets the published address, lab web clients get nginx's
private address. A freshly built firewall forwards routed ports to nginx at once but keeps
the direct split DNS until nginx is ready; firewall-nginx.yml then switches it.
centralIngress enables central firewall GUI ingress and internal web DNS; SSH and DNS
management remain direct. The live helper disables automatic system hosts-file DNS
registration so the firewall's own name has no extra direct LAN answer.
The firewall's final DNS check
resolves the first name of every entry from the PC.
matrix:   matrix = Synapse (Matrix homeserver), Matrix Authentication Service (MAS) and the
LiveKit signalling/JWT service; element = Element Web; @ = lab.internal, which serves
/.well-known/matrix/... for the user IDs @name:lab.internal. 443/80 go through
central nginx to Traefik; TLS certificates remain on each application VM.
7881/tcp and 7882/udp are LiveKit's media ports (voice/video calls). LiveKit
announces the address itself (livekit_server_config_rtc_node_ip in vars.yml):
after changing it here, change it there too and run lab.ps1 deploy matrix.
keycloak: the identity provider (single sign-on); MAS sends browsers there to log in.
rustfs:   S3-compatible object storage at rustfs.<domain> and the UI at rustfs-console.<domain>
over HTTPS on 443; the RustFS backend ports remain private on the VM.
k8s-server: rancher = Rancher Manager, the cluster's management UI; hubble = Hubble UI,
Cilium's view of the network flows between the pods; airflow = Apache Airflow,
deployed by Fleet from fleet/ (lab.ps1 deploy fleet). All through central nginx
to the cluster's ingress (Traefik on k8s-server), for the PC only.
vault:    OpenBao, the secrets manager and certificate authority (PKI); its web UI and API
on 8200 (OpenBao's standard port), e.g. https://vault.lab.internal:8200/ui/, directly
to the VM, never through nginx: OpenBao binds logins to client addresses. Port 80
serves only CA certificates and revocation lists (CRLs): certificates name these
plain-HTTP URLs, and clients such as Windows fetch them to check revocation.
For HTTPS without a warning, every name must also be on the service's TLS certificate (issued by
the lab CA in ansible/playbooks/matrix-prepare.yml, keycloak.yml and rustfs.yml).

ports.description: HTTPS (Traefik: Synapse, MAS, Element, LiveKit signalling)
HTTPS (Keycloak login pages and OIDC endpoints)
HTTPS (OpenBao API, web UI and ACME directory)
HTTP: CA certificates and revocation lists only (nginx allow-list)
HTTPS (Rancher Manager, Hubble UI and Airflow, through the cluster's ingress)
